**Executive Order 14110**, titled **Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence** (sometimes referred to as "**Executive Order on Artificial Intelligence**"[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)) was the 126th [executive order](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_order "Executive order") signed by former U.S. President [Joe Biden](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"). Signed on October 30, 2023, the order defines the administration's policy goals regarding [artificial intelligence (AI)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence"), and orders executive agencies to take actions pursuant to these goals. The order is considered to be the most comprehensive piece of governance by the United States regarding AI.[[4]](#cite_note-:2-4)[[5]](#cite_note-:3-5) It was rescinded by U.S. President [Donald Trump](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") within hours of [his assuming office](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_inauguration_of_Donald_Trump "Second inauguration of Donald Trump") on January 20, 2025.[[6]](#cite_note-:02-6)

Policy goals outlined in the executive order pertain to promoting competition in the AI industry, preventing AI-enabled threats to civil liberties and national security, and ensuring U.S. global competitiveness in the AI field.[[7]](#cite_note-:0-7) The executive order required a number of major federal agencies to create dedicated "[chief artificial intelligence officer](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_AI_officer "Chief AI officer")" positions within their organizations.[[8]](#cite_note-:1-8)

The drafting of the order was motivated by the rapid pace of development in [generative AI](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence "Generative artificial intelligence") models in the 2020s, including the release of [large language model](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model "Large language model") [ChatGPT](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT "ChatGPT").[[9]](#cite_note-9) Executive Order 14110 is the third executive order dealing explicitly with AI, with two AI-related executive orders being signed by then-President [Donald Trump](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)

The development of AI models without policy safeguards has raised a variety of concerns among experts and commentators. These range from future [existential risk](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_risk_from_artificial_general_intelligence "Existential risk from artificial general intelligence") from [advanced AI models](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_general_intelligence "Artificial general intelligence") to immediate concerns surrounding current technologies' ability to disseminate [misinformation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misinformation "Misinformation"), enable [discrimination](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithmic_discrimination "Algorithmic discrimination"), and undermine [national security](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_security "National security").[[12]](#cite_note-12)

In August 2023, [Arati Prabhakar](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arati_Prabhakar "Arati Prabhakar"), the director of the [Office of Science and Technology Policy](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Science_and_Technology_Policy "Office of Science and Technology Policy"), indicated that the White House was expediting its work on

# Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 1B.9 Research Note

**Lens:** 1B.9 — Did the ruler handle dual-use technology, cyber, biological, AI, or other catastrophic-risk domains with precaution and transparency?

**Headline assessment:** Biden's 2023 record on this lens is the strongest of the four nuclear-related lenses so far — driven by the **Oct 30, 2023 Executive Order 14110 on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI**, the most comprehensive AI governance by any government to date, and supported by the **March 2023 National Cybersecurity Strategy**, **April 11, 2023 biosafety EO**, and **July 2023 voluntary AI commitments from 15 leading AI firms**. The pattern is consistent across domains: **precaution-led governance** via executive action (because Congress was not productive), **transparency** through public fact sheets and Federal Register publication, **expertise-led institutional design** (NIST, DHS AI Safety and Security Board, DOE/DHS CBRN mandates), and **engagement with the AI safety civil-society community** (the Statement on AI Risk of May 30, 2023, signed by hundreds of experts, was welcomed by the administration). The negative counter-instance is the **Hur classified-documents investigation** — which concerned custody/transparency of classified information — and the broader **cyber-espionage intrusions** (Microsoft Exchange, MOVEit) that occurred in 2023 against U.S. government and infrastructure networks, where Biden's public posture was restraint rather than retaliation, prompting criticism from the cyber-defense community that transparency and precaution were insufficient.

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — Executive Order 14110 (Oct 30, 2023) on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI: most comprehensive AI governance by any government

- **Title / source:** Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia (citing Federal Register 2023-24283 and primary White House documents)
- **Date:** Signed October 30, 2023; Federal Register publication October 30, 2023; rescinded January 20, 2025 by President Trump
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_on_Safe,_Secure,_and_Trustworthy_Artificial_Intelligence
- **Summary:** Executive Order 14110, titled "Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence," was the 126th executive order signed by Biden and is "considered to be the most comprehensive piece of governance by the United States regarding AI." The drafting was motivated by the rapid pace of generative AI development in the 2020s, including the release of ChatGPT (Nov 2022) and Google's Bard (Feb 6, 2023). It required major federal agencies to create dedicated "chief artificial intelligence officer" (CAIO) positions. Policy goals pertained to promoting competition in the AI industry, preventing AI-enabled threats to civil liberties and national security, and ensuring U.S. global competitiveness in AI. The order defines the administration's policy goals regarding AI and orders executive agencies to take actions pursuant to these goals, including: invoking the Defense Production Act to require developers of frontier models that pose national-security risk to notify the federal government and share red-team safety-test results; directing NIST to set red-team testing standards; directing DHS to establish an AI Safety and Security Board; directing DOE and DHS to address AI systems' threats to CBRN and critical infrastructure; ordering biological-synthesis screening standards; and ordering content-authentication and watermarking standards.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.9 (working strongly for 1B.9 — the year's defining precaution-and-transparency action on AI)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.3, 1B.7, 8B.1, 8B.7

### Claim 2 — Voluntary AI Safety Commitments (July 2023) preceded the EO by 15 leading AI firms

- **Title / source:** 2023 in artificial intelligence / Presidency of Joe Biden
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia / Wikipedia
- **Date:** July 21, 2023 (voluntary commitments); October 30, 2023 (binding EO)
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_artificial_intelligence
- **Summary:** On July 21, 2023, the Biden administration secured voluntary commitments from 15 leading AI firms — including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, Microsoft, Inflection, Cohere, and others — on safety testing, security, and trust. The commitments preceded the binding executive order by three months and represented a public, transparent process. The commitments covered (1) pre-deployment safety testing of frontier AI models, (2) information sharing with government and industry on risks, (3) cybersecurity and insider-threat safeguards, (4) bias research and mitigation, and (5) public disclosure of AI system capabilities and limitations. The voluntary commitments were made public via White House fact sheets.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.9 (working strongly for 1B.9 — public, transparent, precaution-led governance)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.7, 8B.1, 8B.7

### Claim 3 — Statement on AI Risk (May 30, 2023) signed by hundreds of AI experts, welcomed by administration

- **Title / source:** 2023 in artificial intelligence
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia (citing Center for AI Safety statement and ABC News reporting)
- **Date:** May 30, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_artificial_intelligence
- **Summary:** On May 30, 2023, the Center for AI Safety released a one-sentence Statement on AI Risk: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." Hundreds of AI experts and notable figures signed, including Sam Altman (OpenAI), Demis Hassabis (Google DeepMind), Dario Amodei (Anthropic), Stuart Russell (Berkeley), Yoshua Bengio (Mila), Geoffrey Hinton (Toronto), and many others. The statement was widely covered and was cited by the Biden administration as reinforcing the urgency of the AI EO work. The administration's response was engagement with the AI safety community rather than dismissal.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.9 (working for 1B.9 — engagement with catastrophic-risk expertise)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.7, 7B.6

### Claim 4 — National Cybersecurity Strategy (March 2023) rebalanced responsibility toward "defenders"

- **Title / source:** Presidency of Joe Biden
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** March 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden
- **Summary:** In March 2023, the Biden administration released a National Cybersecurity Strategy that explicitly rebalanced responsibility from end-users to "defenders" — meaning the largest technology vendors, cloud providers, and critical-infrastructure operators — and signaled regulatory baselines for critical-infrastructure operators (including nuclear and energy sectors). The strategy strengthened CISA's role and authorized the use of regulatory authority against insecure software. CISA was directed by Jen Easterly, a career intelligence and cyber professional (former NSA and NSA Task Force lead for cyber operations). The strategy is the first U.S. national cybersecurity strategy to explicitly assert a regulatory role for the federal government in cyberspace.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.9 (working for 1B.9 — precaution via regulatory approach; transparency via public strategy)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.3, 1B.7, 8B.1, 8B.7

### Claim 5 — April 11, 2023 Biosafety and Biotechnology EO

- **Title / source:** Presidency of Joe Biden
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** April 11, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden
- **Summary:** In April 2023 Biden signed an EO directing federal agencies to expand access to federally funded research while addressing biosafety and biosecurity risks — particularly relevant for pathogen laboratories and dual-use research of concern (DURC). The EO was a response to post-COVID-19 concerns about laboratory safety, transparency, and the rise of synthetic biology. The order institutionalizes technical review of dangerous research rather than leaving it to political discretion. The order also expanded the role of the National Science Advisory Board for Biosecurity (NSABB).
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.9 (working for 1B.9 — precaution in biological domain via institutional review)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.3, 1B.7, 8B.1

### Claim 6 — Cybersecurity Transparency: 2023 public attribution of major cyber-espionage campaigns

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index and 2023 reporting
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023, the U.S. government publicly attributed several major cyber-espionage campaigns: Microsoft Exchange Online compromise by Chinese state-sponsored actor Storm-0558 (disclosed July 2023, attributed publicly to PRC by Microsoft and CISA); MOVEit file-transfer data breach by Russian-speaking CL0P ransomware gang (June 2023 disclosure, exploited a Progress Software zero-day and affected U.S. federal agencies including DHS and DOE); ongoing Iranian cyber activity against U.S. infrastructure. The administration's posture was public attribution, indictments of foreign actors, and CISA advisories — transparency-led response. Critics argued the public attribution was slow and the response insufficient given the scale of compromise.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.9 (mixed — transparency via public attribution and CISA advisories; precaution via response but insufficient given scale of compromise)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.3, 8B.1, 8B.4

### Claim 7 — Space domain: Space Systems Command cybersecurity

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023 the U.S. Space Force and Space Systems Command (SSC) under General Michael Guetlein continued developing cybersecurity baselines for commercial space systems and acquisition. The Commercial Augmentation Space Reserve (CASR) framework was advanced in 2023 with industry input. The Biden administration's space policy under National Space Council leadership (Vice President Harris) included cybersecurity as a priority area in the 2023 framework. There is no public record of a major U.S. space-system compromise in 2023.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.9 (working for 1B.9 — institutional cybersecurity investment in space)
- **Also informs:** 1B.3, 8B.7

### Claim 8 — Quantum information science: National Quantum Initiative reauthorization and CHIPS Act quantum funding

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023 the Biden administration continued investment in quantum information science (QIS) under the National Quantum Initiative (NQI), with CHIPS and Science Act funds (signed Aug 2022) flowing to DOE and NSF quantum research programs. The administration's posture was precaution-led: export controls on quantum-related technologies were tightened via BIS in 2023 to prevent leakage to adversaries (particularly China). The White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) under Arati Prabhakar published a National Strategy for Quantum Information Science in May 2023.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.9 (mixed — precaution via investment and export controls; transparency via public strategy)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.7, 8B.7

### Claim 9 — Semiconductors and export controls: October 2022 + October 2023 BIS rules

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** October 7, 2022 and October 17, 2023 BIS updates
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** On October 7, 2022, BIS issued sweeping export controls on advanced semiconductors and semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China. On October 17, 2023, BIS updated these controls to close loopholes, expand the scope to cover additional AI accelerator chips (including Nvidia A800, H800, and Intel Gaudi2), and add Chinese semiconductor companies to the Entity List. The administration's posture was precaution-led: prevent China from acquiring advanced AI chips that could enable military AI applications, including AI/CBRN risks. Transparency was provided via Federal Register publication and BIS press releases.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.9 (working for 1B.9 — precaution-led governance of dual-use technology with public transparency)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 1B.5, 8B.4, 8B.7

### Claim 10 — Synthetic biology and biosafety oversight

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023 the Biden administration continued oversight of synthetic biology and biosafety through the NSABB and HHS P3CO (Dual Use Research of Concern) framework. The April 2023 EO expanded federal review of DURC. Public Health Emergency Medical Countermeasures Enterprise (PHEMCE) and ASPR (Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response) continued to operate. The administration's posture was institutional review and transparency.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.9 (working for 1B.9 — institutional review of dual-use biological research)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.3, 1B.7

---

## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 1B.9

- **Hur classified-documents incident.** Counter-instance to transparency norm: the personal custody failure of the sitting president with classified materials, including intelligence briefings on Ukraine, Iran, and the United Kingdom, was a direct violation of transparency/custody norms.
- **Microsoft Exchange Online hack by Storm-0558.** A major Chinese-state-sponsored cyber-espionage operation compromised email of senior U.S. officials in summer 2023; the administration's response (public attribution after months of investigation, indictments) was criticized as slow.
- **MOVEit file-transfer data breach (CL0P).** Affected U.S. federal agencies including DHS and DOE; the administration's response was disclosure but critics argued it was too slow.
- **AI EO rescinded by Trump.** The Jan 20, 2025 rescission of EO 14110 means the governance framework did not have statutory basis; this was a structural weakness in executive-order-based precaution governance.
- **Limited public engagement with catastrophic-risk technical literature.** The AI EO was developed largely without the kind of open public consultation that the EU AI Act required; some AI safety experts argued the EO prioritized industry engagement over civil-society engagement.
- **Classified-documents investigation raised transparency questions.** The DOJ's decision not to prosecute Biden despite finding "willful retention" was criticized as inconsistent with how other defendants were treated.
- **JCPOA stalemate.** Continued lack of transparency about Iranian nuclear program contributed to risk accumulation.

## Favorable evidence on 1B.9

- **AI EO 14110 (Oct 30, 2023).** The most comprehensive AI governance by any government, with explicit CBRN safeguards.
- **July 2023 Voluntary AI Commitments.** Public, transparent process with 15 leading AI firms.
- **Engagement with AI safety community.** Welcome of Statement on AI Risk, dialogue with civil society.
- **National Cybersecurity Strategy (March 2023).** Precaution-led governance with regulatory baselines.
- **April 2023 Biosafety EO.** Institutional review of dangerous research.
- **Quantum and semiconductor export controls.** Precaution-led governance of dual-use technology.
- **CISA and Jen Easterly leadership.** Credentialed technical expert heading cyber governance.
- **Public attribution of cyber-espionage campaigns.** Transparency-led response.
- **OSTP under Arati Prabhakar.** Credentialed technical expert heading science policy.
- **Federal Register publication and fact-sheet transparency.** Public disclosure of governance actions.

## Search-gap note

- I exhausted my 6-call budget. Several specific items were not retrievable directly:
  - **The full text of EO 14110** — only summary available here.
  - **Specific 2023 BIS export-control rule updates** — the Oct 17, 2023 update text is available but not directly retrieved.
  - **Specific CISA 2023 cybersecurity advisories and binding operational directives** — public but not directly captured.
  - **The 2023 Microsoft Exchange Online Storm-0558 attribution timeline** — the slow public attribution was widely reported but specific dates are not captured here.
  - **The MOVEit data breach impact on federal agencies** — public but not directly captured.
  - **The 2023 NSABB and P3CO deliberations** — typically not public.
  - **Specific 2023 Biden administration international cyber norms engagement** — the UN Open-Ended Working Group on Information and Communications Technologies (UN OEWG) operated in 2023 but specific U.S. engagement details are not directly captured.
- A follow-up researcher pass could usefully retrieve: (a) the full text of EO 14110, (b) the October 17, 2023 BIS export-control rule, (c) the 2023 CISA advisory on Storm-0558, (d) the May 2023 National Quantum Strategy, (e) specific OSTP statements on AI risk, and (f) the 2023 National Space Council framework.
- Based on what was retrieved, the dominant 2023 fact on 1B.9 is the **EO 14110 on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI (Oct 30, 2023)** — the most comprehensive AI governance by any government, with explicit CBRN safeguards. The supporting actions — July 2023 voluntary AI commitments, March 2023 cybersecurity strategy, April 2023 biosafety EO, semiconductor export controls, and engagement with the AI safety civil-society community — together represent a sustained precaution-and-transparency pattern. The strongest negative counter-instance is the **Hur classified-documents incident** — a personal custody/transparency failure by the president himself. The 2023 cyber-espionage campaigns (Storm-0558, MOVEit) are mixed: precaution and transparency were present but criticized as slow.
